opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one of the first things we had to confront when we started working on this problem.

The rough way to think about it is that for something to have a smell, it has to physically get to your nose. So the first constraint is volatility: the molecule has to be able to leave a surface or a liquid and float through the air. That immediately rules out a huge chunk of chemical space. Big molecules like proteins or long polymers just don't evaporate at room temperature, so you'll never smell them directly.

In practice, that means odorants tend to be fairly small. Most fall somewhere under about 300 daltons in molecular weight. There are exceptions on the edges, but that's the neighborhood. They also tend to be relatively hydrophobic, though not completely, because once a molecule reaches your nose it has to dissolve into the mucus layer and then interact with olfactory receptors on your sensory neurons. So there's a sweet spot of physical and chemical properties.

The second part is the biology. Even if a molecule is volatile and gets into your nose, it still has to activate at least one of the roughly 400 types of olfactory receptors that humans have. Some molecules are volatile but basically odorless to us. They just don't bind well enough to any receptor, or they bind at concentrations we'd never encounter.

So when we talk about "the space of possible odorants," we mean the intersection of what's volatile, what's small enough, what has the right solubility profile, and what actually triggers our receptors. Even with all those constraints, that space is enormous. Estimates run into the billions of possible molecules, and we've only ever characterized the smell of a tiny fraction of them, maybe a few thousand in a really careful way. That gap is a big part of why we thought machine learning could help. If you can learn the mapping from structure to smell, you can start exploring that huge space without needing a trained human panel to sniff every single molecule.

r001.rationale: The response defines potential odorants through properties such as volatility, size, solubility, and receptor activation. It does not describe enumerating physically realizable molecular structures.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify manufacturability as a filter on potential odorant molecules.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of my favorite questions, because the answer is both really simple and kind of staggering when you sit with it.

The simple version is: a molecule can have a smell if it can get to your nose. That means it has to be volatile, so it has to evaporate at roughly room temperature and float through the air, and it has to be small enough and the right shape to make it into the olfactory epithelium and interact with your receptors. In practice that puts a pretty hard ceiling on size. Almost everything we smell is under about 300 or 350 daltons. Above that, things just don't get airborne in any meaningful concentration. And they tend to be made of a small set of atoms, mostly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, with some nitrogen and sulfur sprinkled in, and occasionally a halogen.

So you can write down those constraints, and then you can ask: how many molecules satisfy them? And that's where it gets humbling. If you enumerate the chemically plausible small organic molecules in that weight range, the number is on the order of tens of billions. Maybe more, depending on how generous you are about what counts as stable. And of those, humanity has characterized the odor of something like five to ten thousand. That's the entire perfumery and flavor industry, a century and a half of work, and it's a rounding error relative to the space.

The way I like to frame it is that vision and hearing have a very low-dimensional input. Light is a wavelength, sound is a frequency and amplitude. You can describe the whole input space with a few numbers. Smell doesn't work that way. The input to your nose is a position in chemical space, which is a discrete, combinatorial, very high-dimensional object. There's no smooth axis you can walk along. You change one atom and sometimes nothing happens, and sometimes you go from grapefruit to rotten egg.

So when we started this work, the goal wasn't really to say "here is the full list of odorous molecules." It was to build a map. If you can learn a function from molecular structure to odor percept, then you can start to lay a coordinate system over that enormous space. You can say, this region smells floral, this region smells musky, and here's where we have never put a single data point. And that's what the principal odor map was trying to be: not a catalog, but a way of navigating a space that's far too big to ever catalog by hand.

r001.rationale: It describes enumerating chemically plausible small organic molecules that meet physical constraints such as volatility and size to define the potential odorant space.

r002.rationale: It mentions stability and physical constraints, but does not identify manufacturability as a filter.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a physical constraint: for a molecule to have a smell, it has to get into your nose. So it has to be sufficiently volatile to leave whatever material it’s in, travel through the air, and reach your olfactory receptors. That tends to put us in the world of relatively small molecules.

But being volatile doesn’t automatically mean something has a smell. It also has to interact with your olfactory system in a way that produces a percept, at the concentration you’re exposed to. So there isn’t a perfectly sharp boundary you can draw just from molecular weight or a few chemical properties.

What you can do is define a plausible space of small, volatile molecules and ask which of them might be odorous. And that space is enormous compared with the set of molecules we’ve actually smelled and characterized. That’s what makes it such an interesting prediction problem: we’ve explored only a small part of the territory.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad space of small, volatile molecules, but does not define it by enumerating physically realizable molecular structures.

r002.rationale: The response mentions volatility and access to the nose as constraints, but does not identify manufacturability as a filter.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by distinguishing all possible molecules from the ones that could actually get into your nose. To smell something, a molecule generally needs to be volatile enough to enter the air, reach the olfactory receptors in your nose, and interact with them. That puts some physical constraints on the space—things like molecular size and vapor pressure.

But those constraints still leave an enormous number of possibilities. And we don’t have a simple rule that lets us look at a molecular structure and say whether it smells, much less what it smells like. Two molecules that look very similar can smell quite different, and molecules that look quite different can smell similar.

So I think of it as a huge chemical space, with a relatively small set of molecules for which we have good human smell descriptions. The challenge is learning how to map from that chemical space into our perceptual experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad chemical space and physical constraints such as volatility, size, and vapor pressure, but it does not define the space by enumerating physically realizable molecular structures.

r002.rationale: The response mentions physical constraints on entering the nose, but does not identify manufacturability as a filter.
